sources.title: Tony Gilroy Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Destroy’ a ‘Healthy and Beautiful Business’ in ‘The Name of Venture Capital’: ‘It’s Tragic’

discussion.body: There’s a self-interest problem worth naming: the man warning that consolidation will destroy a healthy business built his career in the segment he says is disappearing.
Self-interest doesn’t settle the argument, but it does supply the evidence. A $36 million adult drama exists, so the segment isn’t gone — the open question is how many more get made.

items.title: Tony Gilroy Calls the Paramount-Warner Merger ‘Tragic.’ His Film Cost $36 Million.
items.body: Tony Gilroy used the world premiere of his new film to call the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger “tragic” — and the film he was premiering is the argument attached to the complaint. It’s called “Behemoth!”, and it was produced for $36 million. Variety describes it as representative of the mid-budget, adult-oriented drama that once sustained Hollywood’s theatrical business and allowed filmmakers like Gilroy to make a name for themselves. Put those two facts together and a legible worry appears: a merger puts two major studios under one roof, and the tier most exposed to consolidation is the one between the micro-budget and the franchise tentpole — where a filmmaker gets a first shot at something ambitious but not guaranteed, and where there is no obvious defender in a merged studio’s release calendar. Gilroy’s language is a judgment, not a finding. Whether consolidation shrinks that tier is a question about slates and greenlights, answered by release schedules rather than at a premiere. Still, opening a $36 million adult drama is a neat way to make the case: the endangered thing was the film itself.

sources.title: What to know about the Kelvin wave raising the sea level along the West Coast

items.title: A Kelvin Wave Isn’t a Tsunami: It Lifts the Sea Along the Coast
items.body: Kelvin waves are not tsunamis. They don’t curl over and crash on the beach, which is the first thing the word “wave” gets wrong. A better image, as PBS NewsHour puts it, is water sloshing in a bathtub or a swimming pool during an earthquake. The point of that comparison is the motion rather than the cause: a broad displacement of water, not a breaking crest. In the ocean, Kelvin waves are bulges of water that lift the sea level as they move along the coast. The word doing the work there is “along.” The water is raised in a band beside the shore rather than arriving as a wall from open water, which is why the tsunami comparison is the one worth unlearning.

sources.title: Milt Windler, NASA flight director who helped save Apollo 13, dies at 94

items.title: Milt Windler, One of Four Mission Control Leaders on Apollo 13, Dies at 94
items.body: Milt Windler, one of the four leaders of Mission Control who in 1970 directed the round-the-clock effort to bring the Apollo 13 astronauts back to Earth safely, has died at the age of 94. He went on to serve as a flight director for all three crewed missions to Skylab, the United States’ first space station. Four leaders, round-the-clock: that arithmetic is the story. A crisis that unfolds over days isn’t run by one person refusing to sleep; it’s run in shifts, with a flight director holding the room for each one. Windler was one of the four NASA trusted with a leg of it. His later assignment reaches from the most famous rescue in the program to its first space station, a reminder that the work of running a mission outlives the missions everyone remembers.

sources.title: Amazon’s $1B plan to combat data center backlash draws more backlash

discussion.body: The donation is the least interesting number in the announcement. Amazon attached specific promises about power bills and water to it, and those are the two claims a neighbor can actually test.
Test how? “Water positive by 2030” is a standard Amazon defined and a percentage Amazon counted. Self-reported progress is still self-reported.

items.title: Amazon Pledges $1 Billion to Data Center Neighbors, Plus Promises on Bills and Water
items.body: Amazon says it will donate more than $1 billion over the next five years to communities that neighbor its data centers. The company also promised that its data centers wouldn’t increase power bills or wipe out local water supplies, and said it will be “water positive” by 2030, claiming that 75 percent of its projects already meet that goal. Read the two halves separately. The donation is money; the power and water promises are the part a neighbor can check, because a utility bill and a well are not abstractions. And “water positive” is Amazon’s own definition of a standard it says it is meeting — the 75 percent figure is the company’s count, not a third party’s measurement. That structure — a fund, a pledge, a self-reported metric — is now a familiar shape for these announcements. Note what each element does: the donation is discretionary and spread across five years, while the bill and the well are immediate and local.

sources.title: Aaron Sorkin Says “It Never Occurred To Me” That Jesse Eisenberg Wouldn’t Want To Return For ‘The Social Reckoning’

discussion.body: Reading Sorkin’s surprise as vanity misses the more ordinary explanation: he wrote these lines hearing one voice deliver them. Unhearing it is the hard part, not letting go of a paycheck.
Which is exactly the actor’s prerogative. A part can be the thing that defines a writer’s career and still be the thing its performer is done with — and a sequel has to live with that either way.

items.title: Sorkin Assumed Eisenberg Would Return as Zuckerberg. The Sequel Opens Without Him.
items.body: Jesse Eisenberg declined to reprise his portrayal of Meta mogul Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s sequel to “The Social Network” (2010). Deadline describes it as Sorkin logging back into Facebook and finding his friend request denied. The film premieres Oct. 9. What’s notable is Sorkin’s reaction: it “never occurred” to him that Eisenberg wouldn’t want to come back. That reads less like arrogance than authorship — a writer hears his lines in one particular voice, and that voice can be hard to unhear. An actor, reasonably enough, may treat a role as a chapter he has already finished.

sources.title: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war

discussion.body: The sponsorship-to-airstrikes arc is less a betrayal than a bill coming due. Backing an armed movement and directing it were never the same job, and the distance between them is what the current fighting is measuring.
“Former allies” is doing a lot of work in that framing, though. Support is not an alliance, and the word implies obligations that neither side may ever have accepted.

items.title: Pakistan Backed the Taliban for Years. Now It Is Bombing Its Neighbor.
items.body: Pakistan spent years supporting the Taliban in Afghanistan. Now it is bombing its neighbor. Deutsche Welle frames the shift as the story of former allies turned adversaries — and of negotiations that keep failing. Support is not control. A government can spend years cultivating an armed movement across a border and still find that the relationship doesn’t convert into leverage when the shooting starts. That gap between sponsoring a force and steering it is where the interesting, and dangerous, part of this story sits.

sources.title: Internal documents detail Ottawa's economic worries over Alberta referendum

discussion.body: Treating this as a prediction is a mistake. The federal government appears to be costing out a scenario, which is what contingency work looks like, not a forecast of what will happen.
Numbers about separation stop being neutral the moment they exist. Whatever the intent behind them, an internal assessment like this is a political object as soon as anyone can quote it.

items.title: Ottawa’s Internal Papers on the Economic Fallout of Alberta Leaving
items.body: CBC reports that internal federal documents offer a window into how Ottawa is assessing the economic fallout from the possibility of Alberta separating from Canada and becoming an independent state. The paperwork is the story. A federal government costing out the damage of a province’s departure is treating the scenario as something to quantify rather than wave away — and an assessment like this could become ammunition whichever way the politics turns.

sources.title: Inside the study for a remedy to fight Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak

items.title: A Drug Trial Aimed at a Virus With No Approved Vaccine or Treatment
items.body: A drug trial is aimed at Bundibugyo virus, which is responsible for the fast-moving outbreak and has no approved vaccine or treatment. The study began in July and is one of several launched to find some protection — or at least a way to slow the outbreak. That is what outbreak response looks like when the standard tools are missing: the trial itself becomes the intervention.

sources.title: Asghar Farhadi Says Films Like ‘Argo’ Perpetuate American White Savior Myth: ‘Who Asked You to Come and Save Us?’

discussion.body: The load-bearing word is “faithful.” Nobody expects a movie to be a documentary. The objection is that one industry’s version of a country becomes the version everyone outside it absorbs.
That logic would tie every storyteller to their birthplace. Farhadi’s own film is screening in Brazil — work crosses borders in both directions.
Both can be true. The complaint is about a default, not about exchange. An Iranian director showing a film in Rio is a counterexample to the default, not an argument that it doesn’t exist.

items.title: Farhadi in Rio: Hollywood Shouldn’t Be the Reference Point for Other Cultures
items.body: Asghar Farhadi, a two-time Oscar winner, is in Rio de Janeiro for the Rio Film Festival, where he is presenting his film “Parallel Tales.” There, Variety reports, he spoke about what the outlet calls the perceived hegemony of American cinema — and about why Hollywood shouldn’t be treated as a source for faithful portrayals of foreign cultures. (The film is fiction; the argument is the news.)

sources.title: The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy

items.title: The Supreme Court Term Opens Monday With Religion, Guns and Climate Cases
items.body: The Supreme Court’s new term opens Monday, and NPR describes the calendar as carrying big test cases on religion, guns and climate change. NPR adds that the emergency docket keeps coming up as well — the lane where the court is asked to intervene outside the ordinary argument schedule. Three of the most contested areas of American life, plus a channel built for speed rather than full briefing, is a term that will keep the court in the middle of arguments it did not ask to host.

sources.title: Economist Betsey Stevenson breaks down the gender gap in recent hiring reports

items.title: Fewer Jobs Than Expected, and Unemployment Ticks Up to 4.2%
items.body: The U.S. economy added fewer jobs than expected last month, and the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%, per NPR’s report on the latest hiring figures. NPR’s Scott Simon discussed the numbers with Betsey Stevenson, an economist at the University of Michigan. A hiring miss alongside a rising jobless rate points one way: a labor market softer than forecasters had penciled in.

sources.title: 4 Canadians aboard missing Ontario-based air ambulance flying from Bermuda

items.title: Coast Guard Searches for Ontario Air Ambulance Missing With Six Aboard
items.body: The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for an Ontario-based air ambulance jet that went missing with six people on board, four of them Canadians, CBC reports. The aircraft went missing Saturday.

sources.title: Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution

items.title: Two Lethal Injections Failed. Christa Pike Is in Critical Condition
items.body: Christa Pike survived two lethal injections and is in critical condition, the BBC reports, after an execution that failed. Her lawyers said the failure “goes far beyond any one person” — a claim that locates the problem in the process around the execution rather than in a single pair of hands. That framing is the lawyers' argument, not an established finding, but it is the more interesting question: in a procedure built to be irreversible, a botched attempt forces attention onto who, or what, is actually responsible.

sources.title: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 'terrorist attack,' UAE says

items.title: A Co-Pilot Stabbed His Fellow Pilot on an Israel-Bound Flight
items.body: Deutsche Welle reports that a co-pilot stabbed the other pilot aboard a Flydubai flight bound for Israel, and that the man had reportedly been barred from flying in his native Oman over security concerns. That last detail is what lifts the attack out of the category of an isolated in-flight crime: a red flag recorded by one country's authorities, attached to a man flying for a carrier elsewhere.

sources.title: ‘X-Men’s Christopher Abbott Admits He “Hasn’t Read Anything” Yet But “Can’t Wait” To Play Professor X

discussion.body: There is a small, reliable pleasure in a casting announcement that consists almost entirely of willingness. Enthusiasm is cheap and it is not a review; it tells us the actor said yes, not that the part is written.

Willingness is not nothing, though. A performer who signs on before there is a script to read is signing up for the director as much as the character — which makes Schreier the name worth tracking in this announcement.

items.title: Cast as a Mind Reader, Christopher Abbott Hasn't Read Anything Yet
items.body: Christopher Abbott has been cast as Professor X in Marvel Studios' X-Men movie, and he says he is “very much” excited to get to work on it — while still having read nothing for the role. Charles Xavier, famously, reads everyone else's mind; the actor playing him is the one being kept in the dark. Jake Schreier directs.

sources.title: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv

items.title: A Second Bridge Is Struck in Kyiv, After Repeated Attacks on Another
items.body: A strike hit the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge in Kyiv, following repeat attacks on another major bridge in the same city, according to BBC reporting. The detail that stands out is the repetition: this is not a single severed crossing but a run of strikes against the capital's bridges. Bridges are a peculiar kind of wartime target — their damage registers immediately in ordinary life, in commutes, deliveries and evacuation routes, not only on a map of the front.

sources.title: BC NDP and Conservative leaders campaign in the Okanagan

items.title: Eby and Doerkson Take the BC Campaign to the Okanagan
items.body: Global News reports that BC NDP Leader David Eby and Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson were both in the Okanagan on Friday, making campaign promises on grocery prices, wildfire protection and public safety. Two leaders, one region, three files that voters buy groceries, insure homes and call police over.

sources.title: ‘Josephine’ Director Beth De Araújo Delivers Powerful Speech Condemning Cornell Rape Case

discussion.body: An awards stage is a strange place for a request like this, which may be why it lands: the room is full of people who decide what gets made, not just what gets watched.
Peer accountability is the easy half of the sentence. Asking men to police each other can either head off harm or simply move the awkwardness around; the phrase doesn't say which.

items.title: 'Josephine' Director Asks Men to 'Hold Each Other Accountable' at Critics Choice Event
items.body: IndieWire reports that Beth de Araújo, director of “Josephine,” used her Breakthrough Director Award acceptance speech at the Critics Choice Association's Celebración of Cinema & Television to ask men to “hold each other accountable.” Most acceptance speeches are thank-yous with a clock running; this one handed half the room an assignment instead.

sources.title: Paternity is poetical

discussion.body: The sharper objection isn't about hours at all. If becoming a parent changes what you notice and what you can bear to write about, then it has already altered the work — a stronger claim than 'not enemies', and a much harder one to test.

Then test it on the shelf rather than the calendar: the question is whether the poems that exist are worse, not whether the desk was quieter. Swift's side only has to show the conflict isn't necessary, not that it never happens in a given house.

items.title: Daniel Swift Says Fatherhood and Creativity Are Not Enemies
items.body:
The notion that becoming a father costs you your art has the shape of hard-won wisdom: the poems get shorter, the studio goes quiet, and everyone nods knowingly. Daniel Swift's essay argues the opposite, calling that notion 'plain wrong' and saying both poetry and neuroscience are pointing the other way. Note how modest the claim is. He doesn't say children improve the work, only that the two aren't at war — which is the version worth arguing about, because it doesn't rest on any single biography. Work made in a noisy house and work made in a silent study can both count.

What the trade-off story usually smuggles in is a premise about attention: that creativity needs it uninterrupted, and that a child is a rival for it. Once the argument is stated that way, it stops being about love or duty and becomes arithmetic — whose hours, spent how, in what order. And arithmetic is negotiable. A law of nature isn't.

sources.title: Journaling to remember

items.title: Keep a Ledger of the Small Stuff, Not the Headlines
items.body:
Most journals end up competing with the news: the big argument, the diagnosis, the move. Anandi Mishra proposes the reverse — cataloguing the ephemera that slip between the headlines of her days, so that a future version of herself has what she calls a ready reckoner of her life. The point isn't sentimentality. A record of headlines is something anyone holding the same calendar could reconstruct; what's unrecoverable is texture, and texture is what makes an old day feel like it was actually yours.

Writing down the small things is a quietly strange transaction. You do the work now, and the payoff goes to someone who shares your memories but not your mood — future you, who will read the entry the way a stranger reads a found diary, with the advantage of having been there. It's a good argument for keeping the entries boring.
